sets.context:
For more than a century, lichens were understood through a single phrase: a partnership between a fungus and an alga, in which the fungus provides shelter and structure and the alga, by photosynthesis, supplies the sugar. The phrase, repeated in textbooks for generations, had the merit of being short and the demerit of being incomplete. Recent work has shown the lichen to be a considerably more crowded community than the two-partner picture allowed, with a second kind of fungus regularly present and contributing, in ways still being clarified, to the structure long credited to the first.

The discovery did not arrive by accident. Researchers attempting to grow lichens in the laboratory found that combining the textbook fungus and alga produced, repeatedly, something that did not look like a lichen — a growth lacking the characteristic surface chemistry, the typical colours, the recognisable form. The puzzle stood for some years before a second yeast-like fungus, distinct from the first, was identified in the surface tissue of many lichen species. When this fungus was included, the artificial growths began, at last, to resemble the wild material. The phrase about two partners did not, on this evidence, capture what a lichen is.

It would be hasty, on the other hand, to leap from the addition of a partner to a portrait of lichens as freewheeling collectives. The second fungus is not present in every lichen, contributes differently across species, and is itself part of a broader microbial community whose role in the partnership is still being worked out by patient laboratory work. The lesson is not that the old picture was wrong in every detail but that its tidiness was an artefact of how lichens were originally studied, and of which organisms the available techniques were able to recover. Once researchers stopped assuming there were two partners and started looking with newer molecular tools, additional partners turned out to be there.

The case is instructive beyond lichens. A category long held to be settled — 'a fungus and an alga' — was settled in part because the available techniques could not see what they were not looking for. The corrective is not a romance of complexity but a habit of suspecting that the simplest available description may have been favoured for reasons of methodology rather than nature. Most settled categories, given new techniques, prove to be busier than they were thought to be.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?
options: The textbook two-partner picture of lichens is incomplete; recent work has revealed a more crowded community whose discovery illustrates how settled categories can be artefacts of method.
The yeast-like fungus recently discovered in lichen surface tissue is now known to be present in every lichen species that has ever been examined.
Researchers studying lichens in the laboratory have proved that the textbook description of a fungus and an alga is entirely false and should be discarded.
The proper response to the new findings is to abandon the notion of partnership in lichens and treat them as freewheeling microbial collectives without structure.

sets.context:
That the weather of two weeks from now cannot, in any practical sense, be predicted is not a failure of meteorology but a consequence of mathematics. The equations that govern the atmosphere are sensitive to initial conditions in a way that compounds small errors into large ones at a rate set by the system itself; a fractional uncertainty in today's temperature field is, in some number of days, indistinguishable from total ignorance. The deeper insight, established in the 1960s through the work of Lorenz on a deliberately simplified model, was not that prediction is hard but that it is intrinsically bounded — there exists, for systems of this kind, a horizon beyond which prediction is impossible regardless of how good the observations or the computers become.

The result is sometimes misunderstood. Chaos in this technical sense does not mean randomness; the equations are entirely deterministic, with no chance term, and the same initial state, exactly specified, would always evolve in exactly the same way. The unpredictability arises from the fact that initial states cannot be exactly specified — every measurement has a finite precision — and that the system magnifies the unspecified part exponentially. The behaviour is, in the strict sense, deterministic chaos, a phrase whose apparent contradiction dissolves once one notices that determinism and predictability are different properties of the same system.

The misunderstanding matters because it shapes what one expects from improved instruments. A naive reader of meteorology might suppose that better satellites, denser observing networks, and faster computers will, eventually, push the prediction horizon to a month, a year, a decade. The mathematics suggests otherwise. Doubling the observational precision pushes the horizon by a fixed amount whose size depends on the system's growth rate, and for the atmosphere this amount is modest; reaching one extra week of useful prediction requires roughly an order-of-magnitude improvement in precision. The returns to investment in observation are not zero but, after a point, deeply diminishing.

What the picture leaves room for is the prediction of statistics rather than states. One cannot say what the temperature will be in Delhi on a particular day three months hence; one can, given enough understanding of the climate, say something useful about the likely distribution of temperatures over that month. The horizon for statistics is much further out than the horizon for individual states, and a great deal of useful work on weather and climate proceeds in this statistical register. To collapse the two — to treat statistical prediction as a weaker form of state prediction — is to mistake the kind of claim each is making.
